title: The ladder of humility (ch. 7)
hookLine: twelve steps, rising by going down

cards: A ladder is about the simplest machine there is. Put your foot on the bottom rung, push, and you're higher. Up is up.
Nobody has ever climbed a ladder by stepping down it. Chapter seven of Saint Benedict's Rule is built around a ladder, but this one works backward.
On Benedict's ladder, the people who try to climb end up lower, and the ones who step down find themselves rising.

teach.h: WHO EXALTS HIMSELF SHALL BE HUMBLED.
teach.b: Benedict opens the chapter with Jesus's words in Luke, in the Douay-Rheims: "every one that exalteth himself, shall be humbled; and he that humbleth himself, shall be exalted."
Then he reaches back to Genesis, to Jacob asleep on a stone, dreaming of a ladder reaching to heaven, with angels going up and down. Benedict reads the dream his own way.
Going down is what happens when we lift ourselves up; going up is what happens when we bend low. The ladder is our life. Its two side rails are body and soul, and between them God has set the rungs.
Benedict counts twelve. The first is to keep the fear of God before your eyes and never forget it. You've met others this week: obedience is one rung, and holding back from too much talk is another.
Some rungs are gentle: patience when things are hard, being content with the plain and ordinary.

Some are hard for a modern ear, like counting yourself lower than others, and readers today take those steps in different ways. The last rung is humility that shows in the body itself, in how a person walks and stands.

teach.h: TWELVE RUNGS, FROM FEAR OF GOD UP.
teach.b: And the surprise at the top: once all these steps are climbed, Benedict says, the monk arrives at the love of God that casts out fear, quoting the first letter of John: "perfect charity casteth out fear."

teach.h: AT THE TOP, LOVE THAT CASTS OUT FEAR.
teach.b: The ladder starts with fear and ends with love.
Humility, for Benedict, isn't thinking badly of yourself. It's getting out of your own way, until what's left is love, done easily, out of habit and delight.

how: Benedictine monks and nuns hear chapter seven read in community, and some Catholics outside monasteries use its twelve steps as an examination of conscience.

o: never accepting praise or thanks from anyone
rising by stepping down, with love at the top
thinking badly of yourself and your gifts

p: keep the fear of God before your eyes

s: Benedict's ladder of humility ends in self-hatred
he says the climb ends in the love of God that casts out fear.
on Benedict's ladder, you rise by stepping down
lifting yourself up takes you down; bending low takes you up.
Benedict invented the ladder image himself
he draws it from Jacob's dream in Genesis, with angels going up and down.

games.q: you're Benedict, reading Jacob's dream of angels going up and down a ladder. what do you take it to mean?
o: the ladder shows how hard work gets you to heaven.
we go down by lifting ourselves up, and up by bending low.
the angels show that heaven is far away.
games.why: Benedict reads it backward: we go down by exalting ourselves and go up by humbling ourselves.

practice: Look at the day ahead for one small seat you could take that's a step down: letting someone go first, passing the credit to the person who helped, the worse parking spot, the smaller slice.
Picture doing it quietly, without anyone noticing you chose it, and if something in you resists, let it, and breathe out. If you pray, offer that small step down to God.

wordCard.voice: Humility. For Benedict, a ladder you rise on by stepping down, with twelve rungs and love at the top. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, the language of the Rule: humility.

carryVoice: Your line: down is up. On Benedict's ladder, the top rung is love, not fear. Until tomorrow.
